title: Waste nothing
hook: the ban on needless destruction extends to all waste

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was animals first: their meal before yours. Which animal did you tend before your first bite? Today, the last day of the week, a rule that began with a tree. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-eight.

An army is camped around a walled city. The siege drags on. The soldiers need wood for ladders and ramps, and all around them stand fruit trees. The quickest thing would be to cut them all. Deuteronomy stops the axe in mid-air. It's a strange place for an environmental rule, in the middle of a war chapter, but that's where it sits. And from that one verse about fruit trees, the rabbis grew a principle that reaches into your kitchen, your closet, and even the lamp on your table.
screen: `A SIEGE.` → `ORCHARDS ALL AROUND.` → `THE AXE STOPPED IN MID-AIR.`

segments.voice: Bal tashchit. Do not destroy. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. Deuteronomy, chapter twenty: during a siege, "thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them." You may eat from them; you may not cut them down. The rabbis' name for the rule, bal tashchit, echoes that command not to destroy. Second, the tree's own question. The King James renders a short phrase in the verse as "for the tree of the field is man's life." Some readers hear the Hebrew as a question instead: is the tree of the field a person, that it should be besieged by you? Either way, the tree isn't the enemy. It feeds the living, and it has no part in the war. Third, the widening. The rabbis didn't leave the rule in the orchard. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says that someone who makes an oil lamp burn faster than it needs to, wasting the oil, transgresses bal tashchit. Maimonides gathers the principle into law: the same ban applies to one who breaks dishes, tears clothes, wrecks a building, stops up a spring, or ruins food, in a destructive way. A fruit tree became a lamp, a coat, a meal. Fourth, the word that matters: needless. The tradition doesn't forbid using things up. Wood is burned, clothes wear out, food is eaten. What it forbids is destruction for nothing: waste that serves no one. So the question isn't whether to use the world. It's whether this use, right now, has a purpose. Even what is truly yours, in this teaching, deserves a reason before the axe.
screen: `THE AXE AND THE FRUIT TREE.` · `IS THE TREE A PERSON?` · `A LAMP, A COAT, A MEAL.` · `NO DESTRUCTION FOR NOTHING.` · then, large: `WASTE NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reduce one waste. Sit, and breathe. Walk through your day in your mind: the fridge, the tap, the lights left on, the clothes you've stopped wearing, the paper, the packaging, the leftovers. Let one waste stand out, something that serves no one. Don't try to fix everything. Pick one. Decide how you'll handle it today: eat the leftover, turn off the light, give away the coat, mend the shirt. Let it be concrete enough that tonight you'll know whether you did it. The bell holds the time.
Bal tashchit. Do not destroy: a rule about fruit trees in a siege, widened by the rabbis to all needless waste. Today's word.

Your line: waste nothing. Today, take care of the one waste you chose. And look back at the week's lines: holiness is given, human greatness, honest weights, don't steal minds, fair work, animals first, and now, waste nothing. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Bal tashchit is studied as a principle of Jewish law, and some Jewish environmental groups and teachers draw on it when they talk about food waste, energy and caring for the earth.

fork.setup: you're a soldier in a long siege. you need wood, and fruit trees stand all around the city. what does Deuteronomy say?
options: eat from them, but don't cut them down.
burn them so the city can't use them.
fork.reveal: the verse says you may eat from them, but not cut them down. the rabbis built bal tashchit, the ban on needless destruction, on it.

original.note: Hebrew: do not destroy. From Deuteronomy 20:19.

trapdoor: what you thought: waste nothing is about recycling.
what it means: bal tashchit forbids needless destruction of anything useful, from a tree to a lamp's oil.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 20:19, widened in Shabbat 67b and by Maimonides, Laws of Kings 6:10, to vessels, clothes, buildings, springs and food.

notes: Deuteronomy 20:19 quoted twice from KJV; confirm exact wording. Shabbat 67b: covering an oil lamp (making it burn faster) as bal tashchit; confirm source and attribution.
Mishneh Torah, Kings 6:10: the extension to vessels, clothes, buildings, springs and food 'in a destructive way'; confirm.
